subject: english_first_flight
question_text: Why was the young seagull afraid to fly? Do you think all young birds are afraid to make their first flight, or are some birds more timid than others? Do you think a human baby also finds it a challenge to take its first steps?
answer_text: The young seagull was afraid to fly because it was its first flight. It is a well known fact that doing something for the first time is challenging. Therefore, all young birds must be afraid to make their first flights. Similarly, a human baby would also find it a challenge to take its first step.
final_answer: Thus, both young birds and human babies face challenges when attempting new experiences.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of fear in new experiences and drawing parallels.

subject: english_first_flight
question_text: "The sight of the food maddened him." What does this suggest? What compelled the young seagull to finally fly?
answer_text: The young seagull was very hungry. It was this hunger that ultimately compelled it to fly. Its hunger only intensified when it saw its mother tearing at a piece of fish that lay at her feet. It cried to her, begging her to get some food. When its mother came towards it with food in her beak, it screamed with joy and anticipation. However, she stopped midway. It wondered why she did not come nearer. Not being able to resist or control its hunger any longer, it dived at the food in its mother's beak. At that moment, his hunger overpowered his fear of the great expanse of sea beneath the cliff. Finally, this plunge was followed by the natural reaction of its body, i.e., to fly.
final_answer: Therefore, the young seagull's hunger drove it to overcome its fear and fly.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding motivation and emotional response.

subject: english_first_flight
question_text: "They were beckoning to him, calling shrilly." Why did the seagull's father and mother threaten him and cajole him to fly?
answer_text: The young seagull was afraid to fly. Even when it saw its brothers and sisters flying, and its parents helping and teaching them, it could not gather enough courage to make that first flight. That is why its father and mother were calling to it shrilly and scolding it. They threatened to let it starve on its ledge if it did not fly. They did so because they wanted it to leave its fear behind and learn to fly.
final_answer: Thus, the parents used threats to encourage the young seagull to overcome its fear and learn to fly.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding parental motivation and encouragement.

subject: english_first_flight
question_text: "I'll take the risk." What is the risk? Why does the narrator take it?
answer_text: The risk was to fly through the black storm clouds. The narrator took the risk because his home was beckoning him. He was dreaming of his holiday and looking forward to be with his family. He also wanted to get home in time to enjoy a good English breakfast.
final_answer: Thus, the narrator's desire to return home motivated him to take the risk of flying through the storm.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves understanding motivation and risk assessment.

subject: english_first_flight
question_text: Why does the narrator say, "I landed and was not sorry to walk away from the old Dakota…"?
answer_text: After landing, the narrator was not sorry to walk away from the old Dakota because he had a horrific and scary experience flying that plane. He was happy that he had landed the plane safely. That is why he was not sorry to walk away. Instead, he wanted to know where he was and who the other pilot was.
final_answer: Thus, he was relieved and curious after his frightening experience.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of the narrator's emotional state and context of the situation.

subject: english_first_flight
question_text: What made the woman in the control centre look at the narrator strangely?
answer_text: The narrator had asked the woman in the control centre about the identity of the other pilot. She looked at him strangely as there was no other plane in the storm. She told him that no other plane was flying that night. His was the only plane she could see on the radar.
final_answer: Therefore, her reaction was due to the absence of any other aircraft.
difficulty_reasoning: Involves comprehension of the narrative and the situation described.

subject: english_first_flight
question_text: Who do you think helped the narrator to reach safely? Discuss this among yourselves and give reasons for your answer.
answer_text: Probably, it was the narrator's own self that helped him through the storm. There was no other plane in the storm as the woman at the control centre could see only his plane on the radar. Also, no other plane was flying that night. In his fear, he might have been hallucinating. He was a good pilot, and it might have been his own self that came to his help.
final_answer: Thus, it suggests that his own skills and instincts guided him to safety.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires critical thinking and interpretation of the narrative.
